A1.justification: Both PDFs describe A Coefficient Makes SVRG Effective, with matching authors, core methodology and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including v2's additional studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original gradient-variance measurements and training experiments on CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K and eight smaller classification datasets.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds repeated-seed results, learning-rate and schedule comparisons, ResNet-18 experiments and early α-SVRG evaluations.

M1.justification: The central gradient correction and default linear-decay α-SVRG remain unchanged. V2 adds alternative global and within-epoch coefficient schedules and an early α-SVRG variant that operates during the first 10% of training with a transition epoch (Section 5.3, Appendices C.4 and E). These are limited adaptations of coefficient scheduling and application.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-100, Pets, Flowers, STL-10, Food-101, DTD, SVHN and EuroSAT for image classification. The added model configurations and diagnostic experiments reuse these datasets without introducing new task requirements, populations or input environments.

E2.justification: Within matched diagnostic comparisons, v2 removes standard SVRG from Figures 5, 7 and 8, and removes the unmodified SGD baseline from Figure 6. Tables 2 and 3 retain their comparator membership. Replacing the label 'baseline' with SGD or AdamW does not introduce new comparison methods.

E3.justification: V2 substantially expands experimental configurations and controls: ResNet-18 with SGD receives a separate optimization recipe and 50–200-epoch budgets (Appendix C.2, Table 10), both optimizers receive five-value learning-rate sweeps (C.3), and MLP-4 is evaluated for 15/25 epochs on Flowers/EuroSAT (D.1). These are added protocols; the original dataset-specific training budgets are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses compare global and within-epoch schedules, test learning-rate sensitivity and early-only variance reduction, investigate dataset class-count effects, and separate gradient correlation from the standard-deviation ratio (Table 4, Appendices C.3–C.4 and D). The original coefficient-value, batch-size and snapshot-interval analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V1 provides no comparable repeated-run or uncertainty reporting. V2 specifies three-run averages and standard-deviation bands for gradient-variance plots, and Appendix C.2 adds three-seed means and standard deviations for AdamW and SGD experiments in Tables 8–9. This introduces substantial uncertainty reporting without establishing how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive schedule, repeated-seed, SGD, learning-rate and early-variant results. Table 2 replaces the Mixer-S entries: α-SVRG changes from 3.609 training loss and 70.5% accuracy to 3.097 and 76.1%, with baseline and SVRG values also changing. The reason is undisclosed, so this is not an established same-setting performance gain. Revised Figures 7–8 locate variance-reduction benefits primarily in early epochs.

T1.justification: The optimal-coefficient derivation in Section 3 and Appendix A is unchanged. Appendix E adds mathematical definitions of alternative global and double schedules, without a new convergence theorem or proof. Its new Equation 16 conflicts with the stated reset-to-one behavior: the printed expression starts at twice the global linear coefficient.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contribution: smaller, decaying variance-reduction coefficients make SVRG useful for deep neural-network optimization and reduce training loss across vision architectures and datasets. The added studies support this claim and explore variants without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies the variance-reduction benefits in Figures 7–8 as primarily early-training effects. It adds explanations for double-schedule failures and class-count dependence, and attributes coefficient decay mainly to declining gradient correlation (Appendix D.3). Appendix C.4 also discusses roughly doubled computational cost and hypothesizes that restoring late-training gradient noise can benefit generalization.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands implementation documentation through SGD hyperparameters and budgets, explicit schedule formulas and update frequency, early-variant transition details, and SGD/AdamW pseudocode (Appendices C, E and G). Conversely, Appendix B removes the previously documented layer-scale value of 1e-6 without establishing whether the implementation changed. The code-access destination remains unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds a substantive comparison with MARS, acknowledging its related coefficient idea and distinguishing this paper's controlled empirical analysis. V2 also extends variance-reduction references and adds gradient-noise/generalization citations in Appendix C.4. The overall practical, empirical research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: V2 polishes wording, expands explanations of gradient metrics and base optimizers, renames 'snapshot interval' to 'inner loop size', and reorganizes the appendices around additional studies. The main seven-section argument and much of the existing exposition remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Figures 2–3 and 5–8 are redrawn with uncertainty bands, expanded epoch axes and revised displayed comparisons; Figure 8 gains zoomed insets. V2 adds Figures 11 and 13–20, Tables 4 and 8–11, and two algorithm blocks. The original snapshot-interval Figure 11 is retained as Figure 12, rather than removed.

improvement.justification: V1's empirical argument lacked reported replication uncertainty and learning-rate controls. V2 substantially strengthens it with three-seed results, learning-rate and schedule comparisons, and direct analysis of coefficient decay. It also clarifies when variance reduction occurs and discusses computational cost. Removed diagnostic comparators, unexplained Mixer-S replacements and the Equation 16 inconsistency are limitations, but the retained benchmark comparisons and substantial new validation provide a clear net improvement in evidential strength and practical guidance.
